<h1>Electric Eel Drain Cleaning <span class="accent">Sydney</span></h1>
<p class="sh-lead">Electric eel drain cleaning for Sydney lines blocked by roots or anything else that has to be cut rather than flushed. A powered cutting head clears the obstruction, then the camera shows where it got in, so the entry point can be dealt with rather than left. Call any hour, or book online.</p>

<section class="section s-white" aria-labelledby="how-title"><div class="wrap"><div class="head"><span class="eyebrow">Cable and cutting head</span><h2 id="how-title">What an electric eel actually does</h2><p class="lead">Four things worth understanding, because they explain both what this tool is good at and where it is the wrong choice.</p></div><div class="reveal"><div class="rv"><span class="rv-ic"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-rotate"></use></svg></span><h3>A flexible cable, driven under power</h3><p>An electric eel is a steel cable on a powered drum. The drum spins the cable as it is fed into the line, so the whole length rotates rather than just being pushed along.</p></div><div class="rv"><span class="rv-ic"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-bolt"></use></svg></span><h3>A cutting head sized to the pipe</h3><p>Different heads do different work. A root cutter shears through timber and a spade or auger head breaks up compacted material. The head is matched to the pipe diameter and to what the camera found.</p></div><div class="rv"><span class="rv-ic"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-tree"></use></svg></span><h3>It cuts rather than pushes</h3><p>This is the point of the tool. Pushing a root mass along the line relocates the blockage. A spinning cutter removes it, so what comes out is the obstruction rather than whatever was behind it.</p></div><div class="rv"><span class="rv-ic"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-video"></use></svg></span><h3>The line is checked afterwards</h3><p>Cutting roots out does not close the opening they came through. The camera goes back in so you know whether the pipe needs <a href="/services/pipe-relining/">sealing</a> or whether the line is sound.</p></div></div></div></section>
<section class="section s-light" id="when" aria-labelledby="when-title"><div class="wrap"><div class="head center"><span class="eyebrow">Choosing the method</span><h2 id="when-title">When an eel is the answer, and when it is not</h2><p class="lead">Being honest about the second column is what stops you paying twice. A machine that cuts is no use against a coating that needs scouring.</p></div><div class="triage"><div class="tri soon"><b><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-check"></use></svg> An eel is the right tool</b><ul><li><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-check"></use></svg><span>Tree roots growing in through a joint or a crack</span></li><li><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-check"></use></svg><span>Compacted material that has hardened in place</span></li><li><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-check"></use></svg><span>Wet wipes and fibrous matter bound into a mass</span></li><li><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-check"></use></svg><span>Older clay pipe where the bore is rough and material catches</span></li><li><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-check"></use></svg><span>A blockage that has to be cut out rather than flushed through</span></li></ul><div class="tri-act"><a mainEntity.name: What is an electric eel and how is it different from a plunger or a snake?

acceptedAnswer.text: An electric eel is a powered drain machine. A steel cable is driven from a motorised drum so the cable rotates as it travels, and a cutting head on the end shears through whatever is in the way. A hand snake has no power behind it and no cutting action, so it will clear a soft blockage near a fixture but will not touch a root mass in a main line. A plunger moves water, nothing more.

mainEntity.name: Will the cable damage my pipes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Used on a sound pipe with a head sized correctly, no. The cutter is matched to the pipe diameter so it clears the bore rather than working against the wall. On a pipe that has already failed the honest answer is different. If the camera shows a line that is cracked or collapsing, running a cutter through it is not the right job, and you will be told that instead.

Most single blockages are cleared in the same visit. Setting up, running the cable out, cutting through and winding it back is the bulk of the time, and a long main line takes longer than a branch off a fixture.

Yes, unless the opening is sealed. The roots were drawn to moisture escaping through a crack or an open joint, and cutting them out does not close it. The same roots find the same opening again. That is what relining is for. Until the line is sealed, the realistic alternative is cleaning on a planned interval to keep ahead of it.

mainEntity.name: Is an eel or jetting better?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither is better. They do different work. An eel cuts solid obstructions out. Jetting strips coatings off the pipe wall. Roots call for an eel. Grease and silt call for jetting. Where a line has both, the eel goes first to open it and the jetter follows to clean the wall back properly.
